workbook.name: Formal Specification — How to Build an FDPM Plugin
workbook.description: Author-facing specification of the FDPM plugin contract. Covers the manifest shape, the 11 capability kinds the host knows how to invoke, the 4-phase lifecycle (install → enable → activate → disable/uninstall), the in-memory PluginContext surface a plugin sees during activation, the 5 most common failure modes that bite first-time plugin authors, and the formal properties an honest plugin must satisfy (idempotent activation, no host-state mutation outside cap calls, manifest-runtime parity). Companion to SPEC-PLUGGABLE-ARCHITECTURE.md, which is the normative wire-level contract; this workbook is the practitioner's view.

field_values.title: Introduction
field_values.description: Audience, scope, and the relationship between this practitioner spec and the normative SPEC-PLUGGABLE-ARCHITECTURE. Read this if you are about to write your first FDPM plugin and want to know which contracts you must honour.

field_values.title: Vocabulary
field_values.description: Definitions of the four load-bearing terms: Plugin, Manifest, Capability, and PluginContext. Every other section assumes you have read these.

field_values.title: Plugin Lifecycle
field_values.description: The four sequential phases a plugin passes through under the host's control: Install, Enable, Activate, Disable/Uninstall. Each phase declares its inputs (host state, prior phase outputs), outputs (registrations, store rows), and exit condition (when the host considers the phase done).

field_values.title: Capability Surface
field_values.description: The 11 capability kinds the host knows how to dispatch to. Each is documented as a Definition: what it is for, what shape the entry function must have, when the host invokes it, and what registers it through the PluginContext during activation.

field_values.title: Properties, Assumptions, Limitations, Failure Modes
field_values.description: Formal properties an honest plugin must satisfy (idempotent activation, manifest-runtime parity, no out-of-band host mutation). Assumptions the host makes about plugin authorship trust. Known limitations of the v1.2 plugin contract. The five failure modes that most often catch first-time authors.

field_values.title: Worked Example: A Minimal Plugin
field_values.description: An end-to-end walkthrough: the smallest plugin that registers one DomainProfile (one primitive type, one relation type, no validators, no renderers). Anchors every preceding section in concrete code.

field_values.formal: A Plugin is a unit of host-extending code identified by a stable Plugin ID of the form `<vendor>.<name>` (e.g. `fdpm.dnis`, `acme.geospatial`). It consists of (a) a `fdpm-plugin.json` manifest at the package root, (b) an entry module exporting `manifest`, `activate`, and lifecycle hooks, and (c) zero or more capability handler exports referenced by the manifest's `capabilities[]` list. Plugins are loaded by the Host at boot and remain resident until disabled; each plugin has a singleton instance per Host process.
field_values.informal: A bundle of code the Host loads to get new behaviour: new primitive types, new validators, new renderers, new importers and exporters. The manifest is the table of contents; the entry module is the actual code.

field_values.formal: The manifest is a JSON document at the plugin package root with the schema documented in SPEC-PLUGGABLE-ARCHITECTURE §3. Required fields: `id` (Plugin ID), `version` (semver), `spec_version` (which manifest-schema revision the file conforms to), `kind` (server | client | composition), `name`, `description`, `authors`, `license`, `host_compatibility.fdpm` (semver range the plugin supports), `permissions` (array of permission grants the host must approve), `capabilities` (array of capability registrations).
field_values.informal: The plugin's metadata. The Host reads this *before* loading any code, so the manifest must be self-contained — anything that needs a JS expression to compute belongs in the entry module, not here.

field_values.formal: A Capability is a typed extension point exposed by the Host. Each entry in `manifest.capabilities[]` declares: `capability_id` (one of the 11 kinds enumerated in section 4), `local_name` (a per-plugin slug used in logs and CLI listings), `entry` (the named export from the entry module that implements this capability), and an optional `metadata` object whose shape is fixed per `capability_id`. The host validates `entry` resolves to a function/value of the expected shape at activation time; mismatches reject the whole plugin.
field_values.informal: A slot the Host provides and the plugin fills. Examples: 'register a domain profile', 'render markdown for this MIME type', 'validate this primitive type'. Each capability kind has a fixed function signature; the manifest tells the Host which export of the entry module fills which slot.

field_values.formal: PluginContext is the in-memory API surface the Host passes to a plugin's `activate(ctx)` function. It is the **only** legitimate channel for a plugin to mutate Host state. The interface is defined in `src/plugin/types.ts:PluginContext` and exposes (read-only) `pluginId`, `logger`; (mutating) `registerProfile`, `registerValidator`, `registerRenderer`, `registerTransformer`, `registerImporter`, `registerExporter`, `registerExprHelper`. Writes through any other path (direct imports of host internals, monkey-patching, environment-variable side channels) are out-of-contract.
field_values.informal: The Host gives you a `ctx` object. Everything you want to register goes through it. Don't reach around it to import host internals — those are not stable.

field_values.name: Install
field_values.question: How does the Host first acknowledge a plugin's presence on disk?
field_values.inputs: A plugin package directory containing `fdpm-plugin.json` and the entry module, discoverable via the Host's plugin search path (`builtinDirs` + `pluginPaths`). The plugin is not yet present in the Host's loaded set.
field_values.outputs: The plugin's manifest is parsed and validated against the manifest schema. The plugin's `lifecycle_state` is set to `installed` in the Host's plugin registry. The plugin's `onInstall(ctx)` lifecycle hook (if exported) has been invoked exactly once.
procedure: Host walks the plugin search path and finds candidate `fdpm-plugin.json` files.
For each candidate, parse JSON and validate against the manifest schema. Reject malformed manifests with a structured `manifest_invalid` error and skip the plugin.
Check `host_compatibility.fdpm` against the running Host version. Reject incompatible plugins with `host_compat`.
Resolve the entry module path; verify it exists and is loadable. Defer actual import to the Activate phase.
Invoke `onInstall(ctx)` if the plugin exports one. The hook gets a minimal context (logger only); no register* calls are legal here.
Record the plugin in the Host registry with `lifecycle_state: installed`.
field_values.exit_condition: The plugin is present in `host.plugins.list()` with `lifecycle_state: installed` (or `failed` if any of the above rejected). No registrations have occurred yet.

field_values.name: Enable
field_values.question: When does the Host transition an installed plugin to ready-to-activate?
field_values.inputs: An installed plugin (lifecycle_state = `installed`). The Host has decided to enable it (either automatically at boot if `permissions` were already granted, or via an explicit operator action).
field_values.outputs: The plugin's `lifecycle_state` becomes `enabled`. The plugin's `onEnable(ctx)` lifecycle hook (if exported) has been invoked. The plugin is queued for the Activate phase but its capabilities are not yet visible to the rest of the Host.
procedure: Check that all `manifest.permissions` are granted (server-only plugins inherit grants from the Host's trust tier; community plugins may require explicit operator approval).
Invoke `onEnable(ctx)` if exported. Same minimal context as `onInstall` — register* calls are not legal here either.
field_values.exit_condition: The plugin is `enabled` and ready for Activate. Disabling it again at this point is a no-op transition back to `installed`.

field_values.name: Activate
field_values.question: How does the plugin actually contribute its capabilities to the Host?
field_values.inputs: An enabled plugin (lifecycle_state = `enabled`) and its loaded entry module exporting `activate(ctx)`. A fresh PluginContext bound to this plugin's id, with all `register*` methods unlocked.
field_values.outputs: All capabilities declared in `manifest.capabilities[]` are resolved against named exports of the entry module and registered with the Host. The plugin's `lifecycle_state` becomes `active`. Subsequent Host operations (workbook create, primitive validate, render dispatch) include the plugin's contributions.
procedure: Import the entry module (top-level imports run here — keep them cheap).

Call `activate(ctx)`. The plugin uses `ctx.registerProfile(...)`, `ctx.registerRenderer(...)`, etc. to install each declared capability. The host accumulates registrations in the plugin's slot in the registry.

After activate returns, the host cross-checks: every `manifest.capabilities[]` entry MUST have a matching registration. Missing or mismatched-shape registrations reject the activation with `manifest_runtime_mismatch` and the plugin lands in `lifecycle_state: failed`.
On success, set `lifecycle_state = active` and emit a `plugin.activated` event (visible in the host log).
field_values.exit_condition: The plugin is `active`. `host.plugins.listRenderers()`, `host.profiles.list()`, etc. include this plugin's contributions. Activate is idempotent only in the sense that the host refuses to call it twice on the same enabled plugin without a Disable in between.
field_values.branch_condition: If activate throws or any cross-check fails, the plugin transitions to `failed` and ALL partial registrations from this plugin are rolled back atomically. Other plugins are unaffected.

field_values.name: Disable / Uninstall
field_values.question: How does a plugin cleanly leave the Host without leaving registrations behind?
field_values.inputs: An active plugin (lifecycle_state = `active`) plus a Host-driven decision to remove it (operator action, version conflict during reload, or process shutdown).
field_values.outputs: All registrations contributed by this plugin are removed from the Host's tables (renderer registry, validator registry, profile registry, etc.). Workbooks already constructed against the plugin's profile are NOT mutated; they remain on disk and become un-loadable until the plugin is re-activated. The plugin's `lifecycle_state` becomes `disabled` (Disable) or removed entirely from the registry (Uninstall).
procedure: Invoke `onDisable(ctx)` if exported. The plugin gets a chance to flush in-flight work, but cannot register anything new.
Host removes every registration whose `pluginId` matches this plugin from every registry table. The removal is atomic (other plugins observe a consistent state).
On Uninstall: invoke `onUninstall(ctx)`, then remove the plugin entry from the Host registry entirely.
field_values.exit_condition: The plugin's `pluginId` no longer appears in any registry. Workbooks created against the plugin's profile are inert until the plugin is re-installed and re-activated.

field_values.formal: Manifest entry: `{ "capability_id": "cap:profile", "local_name": "<slug>", "entry": "PROFILE" }`. The named export must be a `DomainProfile` value (not a function). Activation calls `ctx.registerProfile(PROFILE)`. Registers the typed vocabulary (primitive types, relation types, scopes, categories, validation rules, templates, renderer bindings) against the Host's profile registry. Most plugins ship exactly one cap:profile entry.
field_values.informal: Without this, there is nothing for workbooks bound to your profile to validate against. The profile id is your contract with every workbook that uses you — never bump it for additive changes (see property:profile-id-stability).

field_values.formal: Manifest entry: `{ "capability_id": "cap:renderer", "local_name": "<slug>", "entry": "<exportName>", "metadata": { "renderer_id": "<plugin-prefixed:RendererName>", "target": "text/markdown|application/x-yaml|...", "output_path": "<suggested-filename>" } }`. Entry must be a `RendererFn` accepting `RendererInput` (workbook + primitives + relations + templates + profile) and returning `{ contentType, bytes }`. Invoked over MCP via `fdpm://workbook/{id}/render/{target}` or via `fdpm render --workbook X --target Y`.
field_values.informal: Renderers MUST be deterministic — same workbook revision in, same bytes out — because the host caches by content hash. Read-only by construction; do not call back into the Host.

field_values.formal: Manifest entry: `{ "capability_id": "cap:validator", "local_name": "<slug>", "metadata": { "rule_id": "<plugin-prefix>:val:<name>", "type_id": "<plugin-prefix>:<TypeName>" } }`. Entry must be a `ValidatorFn` with signature `(ctx: ValidatorContext, instance: Primitive) => ValidationFinding[]`. Implements rules whose predicate cannot be expressed in pure CEL.
field_values.informal: Use this only when CEL is genuinely insufficient (a regex over a corpus, a stateful cross-primitive check the CEL activation does not expose). Plain-CEL rules belong in the profile's `validation_rules[]` instead.

field_values.formal: Manifest entry: `{ "capability_id": "cap:lifecycle-hook", "local_name": "on-install|on-enable|on-disable|on-uninstall", "entry": "<exportName>" }`. Entry must accept a minimal `(ctx)` and may be async. Invoked exactly once per state transition.
field_values.informal: Hooks MUST NOT call register* methods on `ctx` — those are only legal inside `activate(ctx)`. Keep hooks cheap (sub-100 ms); they block host boot.

field_values.formal: Manifest entry: `{ "capability_id": "cap:transformer", "local_name": "<slug>", "metadata": { "from_type_id": "<src>", "to_type_id": "<dst>", "name": "<plugin-prefix>:<verb-name>" } }`. Entry is a `TransformerFn` returning `TransformerOpEmission[]` — a list of intended primitive/relation create operations the host commits as one atomic batch. Used for one-shot lifts (e.g. `sw:Capability` -> `sw:Endpoint` skeleton) and migration steps.
field_values.informal: Transformers MUST NOT directly mutate the workbook; they emit ops and let the host commit them. This keeps the operation log honest and makes transforms reversible.

field_values.formal: Manifest entry: `{ "capability_id": "cap:importer", "local_name": "<slug>", "metadata": { "format": "<format-id>", "description": "<short>" } }`. Entry is an `ImporterFn(input: Buffer | string, opts: ImporterOptions) => Promise<ImporterResult>` returning the workbook id, op log, and any warnings. Each plugin can register one importer per `format` string.
field_values.informal: The importer must validate against the bound profile before returning. Partial-import semantics are out-of-contract; if the source contains unrepresentable content, return warnings rather than dropping silently.

field_values.formal: Manifest entry: `{ "capability_id": "cap:exporter", "local_name": "<slug>", "metadata": { "format": "<format-id>", "description": "<short>" } }`. Entry is an `ExporterFn(workbook: WorkbookSlice, opts: ExporterOptions) => Promise<ExporterResult>` returning bytes + suggested filename. Mirror of cap:importer.
field_values.informal: Determinism is required: same workbook in, same bytes out. Round-trip with the matching importer is a property worth testing but is not enforced by the host.

field_values.formal: Manifest entry: `{ "capability_id": "cap:expr-helper", "local_name": "<slug>", "metadata": { "helper_id": "fn.<plugin-id>.<name>", "arity": <integer> } }`. Entry is an `ExprHelperRegistration` with `evaluate(args: unknown[]) => unknown`. Becomes callable from CEL expressions in validation rules.
field_values.informal: The helper MUST be pure and bounded — no I/O, no unbounded loops. CEL evaluation is on the request hot path. Namespacing the helper id under your plugin id (`fn.<plugin-id>.<name>`) makes collisions impossible.

field_values.formal: Manifest entry: `{ "capability_id": "cap:template", "local_name": "<slug>", "metadata": { "template_id": "<plugin-prefix>:tpl:<name>", "target_renderer": "<RendererId>" } }`. The template definition itself lives inside the registered DomainProfile under `templates[]`; this manifest entry just makes it discoverable.
field_values.informal: Templates have no executable code — they are data. Their job is to declare which renderer interprets them and what rendering rules (voice, tense, max depth) apply.

field_values.formal: Manifest entry: `{ "capability_id": "cap:asset", "local_name": "<slug>", "metadata": { "src": "<relative-path-from-plugin-root>", "dst": "<relative-path-in-dist>" } }`. No `entry` field. Declares a non-code asset (CSS, font, schema JSON, image) that the Host's bundler must copy from the plugin source to the dist tree at build time.
field_values.informal: Used sparingly. Most plugins do not ship assets. When they do (a renderer that needs a custom font, an importer that needs a schema JSON), this is how the file makes it into the runtime tree.

field_values.formal: Some legacy plugin manifests separated format-declaration metadata from the importer function for clarity. v1.2 hosts accept the combined form (cap:importer carrying the metadata directly). Legacy hosts that recognise this kind treat it as pure metadata with no `entry` field.
field_values.informal: Use cap:importer directly in new plugins. The separate format declaration is preserved for backwards-compatibility readers, not new authors.

field_values.name: Idempotent Activation Sequence
field_values.claim: For any plugin P, the sequence (Install -> Enable -> Activate -> Disable -> Enable -> Activate) MUST leave the Host in a state functionally indistinguishable from (Install -> Enable -> Activate). All registrations contributed by P after the second Activate MUST equal the registrations contributed after the first Activate, modulo internal ULIDs assigned by the host.
field_values.intuition: The Host promises atomic rollback on Disable: every registration made by the plugin is removed when it is disabled. The plugin's `activate(ctx)` therefore re-runs from a clean slate on re-enable, and a deterministic activate produces the same result. If your activate is not deterministic (reads a timestamp, generates a random id), you are violating this property.
field_values.caveat: If the plugin keeps state outside the Host (a cache file, a remote handle), restoring functional equivalence depends on the plugin's own teardown in `onDisable`. The Host can only guarantee its side of the contract.

field_values.name: Manifest-Runtime Parity
field_values.claim: Every entry in `manifest.capabilities[]` MUST resolve to a named export of the entry module that matches the expected shape for its `capability_id`. Conversely, every `ctx.register*` call inside `activate(ctx)` MUST correspond to a manifest entry. Asymmetry is rejected at activation time.
field_values.intuition: The manifest is the contract. The host validates BOTH directions: (a) declared-but-not-implemented = `manifest_runtime_mismatch` rejection; (b) implemented-but-not-declared = the registration is dropped silently in v1.x, treated as a hard error in v2.0. Treat the v1.x behaviour as already-deprecated.
field_values.caveat: Cap:asset entries have no `entry` field and no register* counterpart — they are bundler directives, not runtime registrations. They do not participate in this parity check.

field_values.name: No Out-of-Band Host Mutation
field_values.claim: A plugin MUST NOT mutate Host state through any channel other than the methods exposed on its `PluginContext`. In particular, plugins MUST NOT import `src/core/store/*` or `src/core/host.ts` directly, monkey-patch host objects, or perform side-effects via shared globals.
field_values.intuition: PluginContext is the supported surface. Anything else is a host implementation detail subject to change between minor versions. Plugins that reach around it become un-upgradable.
field_values.caveat: Reading host *types* (interfaces, type aliases) from `src/core/models/meta.ts` and `src/plugin/types.ts` is fine and expected — the type-only imports are the contract. The boundary is between reading shapes (allowed) and calling methods or mutating singletons (not allowed).

field_values.name: Profile ID Stability Under Additive Changes
field_values.claim: For any two plugin versions V1 and V2 of the same plugin, if V2 is additive over V1 (no primitive/relation removed, no required field added, no enum value removed) then `PROFILE.id` MUST be unchanged. Only breaking changes (removal, required-field tightening, semantic redefinition) MAY bump the profile id.
field_values.intuition: Workbooks pin themselves to `profile_id`. If the id changes, every existing workbook becomes orphaned. Bumping `manifest.version` and `PROFILE.version` separately from `PROFILE.id` lets the Host serve old and new workbooks under one plugin version.
field_values.caveat: Some plugins shipped a slow start that violates this (e.g. early `software-architecture` revisions bumped the id while making additive changes). Treat those as historical mistakes; new plugins should not repeat them.

field_values.name: Lifecycle Hooks Are Side-Effect Bounded
field_values.claim: Each lifecycle hook (`onInstall`, `onEnable`, `onDisable`, `onUninstall`) is invoked exactly once per transition through its corresponding state edge. Hooks MUST be idempotent across retries (the Host may retry on transient I/O failure) and MUST complete within the Host's lifecycle-hook timeout (default 5 s).
field_values.intuition: Hooks run on the Host's hot path during boot or operator action. A hook that opens a network connection, reads a remote schema, or waits on a lock blocks every subsequent plugin's activation. Keep them cheap.
field_values.caveat: Async hooks (returning a Promise) are awaited; the timeout applies to the awaited resolution. Throwing inside a hook transitions the plugin to `failed` and the next operator action is the only path forward.

field_values.name: Plugins are authored by trusted parties (v1-v2)
field_values.statement: The v1 and v2 plugin contract assume `core` trust tier for every plugin. The manifest `permissions` field is recorded but not enforced against a sandbox. Plugin authorship is therefore restricted to FDPM contributors and verified vendors until the trust-tier hardening described in PURPOSE.md ships. A future v3 contract will add capability gating, signature verification, and a sandboxed execution context for community plugins.

field_values.name: Each plugin is a singleton per Host process
field_values.statement: The Host loads each plugin id exactly once. Re-loading a plugin from a different on-disk path with the same id is rejected as a conflict. This assumption simplifies registration tables (one row per pluginId per registry) but means hot-reload requires a full Host restart.

field_values.name: Plugins target the Host's Node.js runtime
field_values.statement: Plugins are TypeScript compiled to ESM JavaScript and loaded via dynamic `import()`. They have access to the Node.js standard library and the Host's process-level resources (file system, network) within whatever the operator has granted. WASM plugins, browser-only plugins, and language-other-than-TS plugins are out of scope for v1-v2.

field_values.description: The Host does not hot-reload plugins. After editing plugin source, the operator must rebuild (`npm run build` in `fdpm-cli/`) and restart the Host (the MCP server, the CLI process, or whatever consumes it). The four lifecycle hooks fire only on explicit transitions, never on file-system change.

Plugins cannot declare dependencies on other plugins in the manifest. The composition profiles (`profile:formal-specification-dnis:0.1`, `profile:spec-authoring-dnis:0.1`) achieve composition by reading the other profile at activation time and panicking if it is absent — but there is no manifest-level `requires: [other-plugin-id]` field. v3 should add this.

For most capability kinds (cap:profile, cap:transformer, cap:expr-helper) the Host accepts multiple registrations from one plugin only when the metadata distinguishes them (e.g. different `helper_id`). For cap:renderer the disambiguator is `(target, renderer_id)` — two renderers with the same target but different renderer_ids both register, but the client must pass `--renderer-id` to disambiguate at invocation time.

Plugins cannot read user-supplied configuration. The manifest is fully static; there is no per-instance config file the operator can edit. Behaviour variation must be done either through environment variables (which the plugin reads explicitly inside its handlers) or by shipping multiple manifest files. v3 should add a `manifest.config_schema` + `host.plugins.configure(pluginId, values)` pair.

field_values.condition: The plugin's `activate(ctx)` registers a renderer that the manifest did NOT declare in `capabilities[]`, OR the manifest declares a capability whose entry-export does not exist on the entry module.
field_values.recovery: Run `fdpm plugin diagnose <plugin-id>` (when available) or read the Host log; the cross-check produces a `manifest_runtime_mismatch` finding listing exactly which entries failed. Fix by either declaring the capability in the manifest or removing the orphan register* call.

field_values.condition: An additive plugin upgrade bumps `PROFILE.id` (e.g. `:1.0` -> `:1.1`) along with the manifest version. Existing workbooks bound to `:1.0` fail to load against the new build with `unknown_profile`.
field_values.recovery: Revert the id bump; bump only `version`. If the bump is already in production, ship a migration that rewrites every workbook's `profile_id` field. The migration is operator-run; the Host does not auto-rewrite.

field_values.condition: A renderer reads `Date.now()`, generates a random UUID, or otherwise emits non-deterministic bytes. The Host's content-hash cache thrashes; downstream consumers see the workbook as `dirty` on every call.
field_values.recovery: Audit the renderer for sources of non-determinism. If a timestamp is genuinely needed (e.g. ADR `last_reviewed_at`), source it from a primitive's field rather than the wall clock. Determinism is verifiable: render the same workbook twice; the bytes must equal.

field_values.condition: An `onInstall` or `onEnable` hook performs a synchronous I/O call that blocks for tens of seconds (DNS lookup of a remote schema, awaiting a slow lock). Host boot stalls; other plugins' activations queue behind this one.
field_values.recovery: Move the slow work out of the lifecycle hook into either (a) lazy initialisation inside the actual capability handler (most renderers can lazily build their state on first call) or (b) a background task the plugin starts in `activate` but does not await. Lifecycle hooks should be sub-100 ms.

field_values.condition: The plugin imports from `src/core/store/store.ts` or `src/core/host.ts` and calls a private method to bypass `PluginContext`. The plugin works in v1.x but breaks on the next minor release when the imported symbol moves.
field_values.recovery: Refactor to use `ctx.register*` exclusively. If your use case genuinely cannot be served by the existing PluginContext surface, file an issue against SPEC-PLUGGABLE-ARCHITECTURE proposing a new method — the host maintainers would rather extend the contract than have plugins reach around it.

field_values.name: Plugin Author
field_values.responsibilities: Authors the manifest and the entry module; satisfies the formal properties of section 5; observes the lifecycle phases; honours the failure-mode mitigations. The author is the audience of this specification.

field_values.name: FDPM Host
field_values.responsibilities: Loads plugins from the discovery path, runs lifecycle hooks, validates manifests, dispatches calls to capability handlers, atomically rolls back failed activations. Implementation: `src/plugin/runtime.ts` and `src/plugin/context.ts`. The host is the counterparty in every contract this spec describes.

field_values.title: src/plugin/types.ts (TypeScript surface for PluginContext, RendererFn, ValidatorFn, etc.)
fdpm-cli/plugins/dnis (smallest reference plugin: one DomainProfile, two primitive types, two relation types)
Documentation Obligations for Approval
field_values.description: Two artifacts every newly approved plugin SHOULD provide: a Product Page (a substantive README at the plugin source root explaining what the plugin does to a non-developer reader) and a View Page (the profile-derived workbook view, exposed via cap:profile and consumed by the web frontend). The MCP server SHALL expose both as read-only resources at fdpm://plugin/{plugin_id}/product-page and fdpm://workbook/{workbook_id}/view-page. Approval is human-reviewed; existing plugins are grandfathered until their next minor version bump. The obligation is a documentation contract, not a load-time gate.

field_values.formal: A user-facing narrative document at <plugin-root>/README.md (or a manifest-pointed alternative if a future schema field exists). The document SHOULD explain, for a non-developer reader: (a) what the plugin does, (b) when to use it, (c) what its profiles model and what cap:renderer outputs to expect, (d) the cost (declared permissions, helper-set or host pinning constraints). The MCP server reads the file from the plugin source root (resolved via plugin.get's source.root field) and exposes it verbatim as text/markdown at fdpm://plugin/{plugin_id}/product-page. Empty or template-only README is not a satisfied obligation; reviewers SHOULD reject. Two of the seven in-tree plugins ship a substantive README today (formal_specification, planning); the remaining five are grandfathered.
field_values.informal: Think of it as the page someone lands on when they search 'what does fdpm.<your-plugin-name> do?' before they decide to enable it. If the reader still does not know after reading, the obligation is not met.

field_values.formal: A workbook-renderable surface derived from the plugin's cap:profile contribution. Plugins that contribute at least one cap:profile SHOULD treat the profile's primitive_types and relation_types as the public schema that the web frontend's generic group-by-type renderer can display without further plugin code. The MCP server SHALL expose a per-workbook synthesised Markdown summary at fdpm://workbook/{workbook_id}/view-page (text/markdown), enumerating workbook metadata, primitive counts by type, and active relations. Plugins that wish to ship a richer client-side view MAY declare a cap:ui:* capability per the manifest schema (cap:ui:primitive-card, cap:ui:renderer-preview, etc.); host-side dispatch for cap:ui:* is not implemented as of v1.1, and these declarations are forward-compatible only. Plugins that contribute no cap:profile (e.g., adapter-only plugins like fdpm.dnis when treated purely as a SPEC-CORE adapter) MAY skip the View Page obligation.
field_values.informal: The View Page is what someone sees when they open a workbook bound to your profile in the web frontend. For most plugins, it is satisfied automatically the moment a cap:profile is registered — the profile's typed schema makes the workbook renderable. The obligation is to ensure that profile is rich enough to be self-explanatory at the workbook level.

field_values.formal: MCP resource URI. resources/list emits one entry per loaded plugin. resources/read returns { contents: [{ uri, mimeType: 'text/markdown', text: <readme-bytes> }] }. The server reads the README from <source.root>/README.md (where source.root comes from the plugin's runtime record, see plugin.get). If the file is missing or empty, resources/read returns category=not_found with reason=missing_product_page; resources/list still emits the entry as a discoverability signal that the plugin has not satisfied the obligation. The resource is idempotent and read-only.
field_values.informal: Designed to be cheap to call — the README is read from disk on each request, no caching, no rendering. Markdown is shipped to the client unchanged.

field_values.formal: MCP resource URI. resources/list emits one entry per loaded workbook. resources/read returns { contents: [{ uri, mimeType: 'text/markdown', text: <synthesised-markdown> }] }. The text is a deterministic Markdown rendering of the workbook's identity (id, name, profile_id, revision), primitive counts grouped by type_id, and relation counts grouped by type_id. Determinism property: same workbook revision in, same Markdown out. Synthesis is server-side; the workbook's plugin contributes no executable code to the View Page beyond having registered the cap:profile that defines the type vocabulary the synthesis enumerates.
field_values.informal: This is the workbook-level analogue of fdpm://plugin/{id}/product-page — a generated Markdown summary aimed at human reviewers and MCP clients without a frontend. Plugins that want a richer per-workbook view should ship a web-frontend template (today: separately, in the web package; tomorrow: via cap:ui:* once host-side dispatch lands).

field_values.name: Approval Readiness
field_values.claim: A newly-submitted plugin P is approval-ready if and only if both (1) fdpm://plugin/{P.id}/product-page resolves with a non-empty Markdown body via resources/read, and (2) for every cap:profile capability c declared by P with profile_id pid, a workbook bound to pid resolves fdpm://workbook/{wb}/view-page with a non-empty Markdown body via resources/read. P with zero cap:profile contributions is approval-ready iff condition (1) holds.
field_values.intuition: The two MCP resources function as approval evidence. A reviewer (human, today) can verify both URIs return content before approving. The condition is mechanical and reproducible — point an MCP client at the running fdpm-mcp, ask it for both resources, check the output is non-empty Markdown.
field_values.caveat: The property does not test prose quality; it tests artifact presence. A README full of lorem ipsum satisfies condition (1) on a literal read. Reviewer judgment is therefore still required — automation gates artifact existence, not coherence. Existing in-tree plugins are grandfathered (see assumption:grandfather-existing-plugins) and are NOT required to satisfy this property until their next minor version bump.

field_values.name: Plugin approval is human-reviewed
field_values.statement: Plugin approval as of v1.x is a human review step. There is no CI gate that checks the Product Page and View Page resources before merge or release. The MCP server returns the resources at runtime; a reviewer points an MCP client at fdpm-mcp and verifies both URIs return non-empty Markdown bodies. A future automated gate (a script that boots fdpm-mcp, calls resources/read on both URIs, and fails CI on missing content) is feasible but not committed.

field_values.name: In-tree plugins are grandfathered until next minor bump
field_values.statement: The seven in-tree plugins as of this section's authoring (fdpm.dnis, fdpm.formal-specification, fdpm.formal-specification-dnis, fdpm.planning, fdpm.software-architecture, fdpm.spec-authoring, fdpm.spec-authoring-dnis) are NOT required to retroactively satisfy property:approval-readiness. Two of the seven (formal_specification, planning) ship a substantive README at source root; five do not. The obligation applies to (a) plugins submitted after this section is published, and (b) any in-tree plugin at its next minor version bump. Grandfathering is a one-time concession to keep the obligation introduction non-breaking.

field_values.description: The MCP server cannot reject a plugin at load time for missing Product Page or View Page resources. The Host's plugin loader runs before any MCP client has had a chance to call resources/read; even if it could, refusing to load a plugin because its Markdown is empty would be a destructive cure for a documentation gap. The obligation is enforceable only at approval-review time (a human looks at the resource bodies) or via a CI script (a hypothetical, not-yet-shipped gate that boots fdpm-mcp and asserts the resources resolve). Plugins that fail the obligation still load and operate; the only consequence is that fdpm://plugin/{id}/product-page returns category=not_found.

field_values.condition: A plugin is approved without the Product Page and View Page MCP resources resolving. resources/list emits the URIs but resources/read returns not_found; the web frontend falls back to manifest-only and generic-group-by-type views.
field_values.recovery: Ship a substantive README at <plugin-root>/README.md (Product Page) and ensure cap:profile registers a sufficiently rich primitive_types set (View Page). Reviewer SHOULD reject re-approval until both resources resolve.
